questions.q: Which enzyme is deficient in classic phenylketonuria (PKU)?
questions.explain: Classic phenylketonuria is caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, preventing the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.

open.q: Name the enzyme deficient in classic phenylketonuria.

questions.q: Why does tyrosine become a conditionally essential amino acid in patients with classic phenylketonuria?
options: Tyrosine cannot be absorbed from food
Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency prevents tyrosine synthesis from phenylalanine
Tyrosine is degraded by homogentisate oxidase
questions.explain: In healthy individuals, tyrosine is synthesized by hydroxylating phenylalanine; when phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient, dietary tyrosine becomes essential.

open.q: Explain why tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid in patients with classic phenylketonuria.
accept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency blocks endogenous conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine
Tyrosine cannot be synthesized from phenylalanine

questions.q: Which cofactor deficiency causes malignant (atypical) phenylketonuria that fails to respond to dietary phenylalanine restriction alone?
questions.explain: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is an essential cofactor not only for phenylalanine hydroxylase but also for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so its deficiency impairs catecholamine and serotonin synthesis.

open.q: Name the cofactor whose deficiency causes malignant phenylketonuria with severe neurotransmitter depletion.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain, bluish-black pigmentation of the pinnae and sclerae, and urine that darkens upon standing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate oxidase deficiency in tyrosine catabolism; accumulated homogentisic acid oxidizes to a dark pigment (ochronosis) in cartilage and urine.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes alkaptonuria, characterized by ochronosis and urine turning dark on standing?

questions.q: Oculocutaneous albinism type 1 is most commonly caused by a deficiency of which copper-containing enzyme?
questions.explain: Tyrosinase catalyzes the oxidation of tyrosine to DOPA and dopaquinone in melanocytes; its deficiency impairs melanin biosynthesis.

open.q: Name the enzyme deficient in classic oculocutaneous albinism.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, renal tubular acidosis, and a cabbage-like body odor. Urine succinylacetone is markedly elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Hereditary tyrosinemia type I is caused by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency, leading to accumulation of toxic fumarylacetoacetate and succinylacetone, which causes liver failure, Fanconi syndrome, and hepatocellular carcinoma risk.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes hereditary tyrosinemia type I with elevated succinylacetone and a cabbage-like odor?

questions.q: How does nitisinone (NTBC) treat hereditary tyrosinemia type I?
options: It inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, reducing toxic metabolite formation
questions.explain: Nitisinone inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, halting the tyrosine catabolic pathway upstream before maleylacetoacetate, fumarylacetoacetate, and succinylacetone can form.

open.q: Name the upstream enzyme inhibited by nitisinone in the treatment of hereditary tyrosinemia type I.

questions.q: A 6-day-old term neonate develops poor feeding, vomiting, alternating hypertonia and hypotonia, and urine smelling of burnt sugar. Plasma levels of leucine, isoleucine, and valine are markedly elevated. Which enzyme complex is deficient?
questions.explain: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is caused by branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) deficiency, impairing decarboxylation of alpha-ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine, and valine.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme complex causes maple syrup urine disease?

questions.q: A 14-year-old tall, slender boy with arachnodactyly presents with downward and inward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), intellectual disability, and a deep vein thrombosis. Which enzyme is most commonly deficient?
questions.explain: Classic homocystinuria is caused by cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, presenting with Marfanoid habitus, downward lens dislocation (vs upward in Marfan syndrome), intellectual disability, and thromboembolism.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme is the most common cause of classic homocystinuria?

questions.q: Cystinuria is caused by a defective renal proximal tubular and intestinal dibasic amino acid transporter that impairs reabsorption of cystine along with which three other amino acids?
questions.explain: Cystinuria affects the COLA transporter (Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine); poorly soluble cystine precipitates in acidic urine to form hexagonal cystine kidney stones.

open.q: Name the three dibasic amino acids whose renal reabsorption is impaired alongside cystine in cystinuria.

questions.q: Hartnup disease presents with pellagra-like photosensitive dermatitis, cerebellar ataxia, and aminoaciduria due to defective intestinal and renal transport of which neutral amino acid?
questions.explain: Hartnup disease is caused by a defect in the SLC6A19 neutral amino acid transporter, impairing tryptophan absorption and reducing endogenous NAD+/niacin synthesis.

open.q: Impaired absorption of which essential amino acid causes the pellagra-like symptoms seen in Hartnup disease?

questions.sub: Organic Acidemias and Urea Cycle Defects
questions.q: Which two vitamin cofactors are required sequentially to convert propionyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA?
questions.explain: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase requires biotin to form methylmalonyl-CoA, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12) to form succinyl-CoA.

open.q: Name the two vitamins required as cofactors by propionyl-CoA carboxylase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

questions.sub: Organic Acidemias and Urea Cycle Defects
questions.q: A 4-day-old male infant presents with vomiting, lethargy, tachypnea, severe hyperammonemia, low plasma citrulline, and elevated urinary orotic acid. What is the inheritance pattern and deficient enzyme?
options: Autosomal recessive; carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
questions.explain: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the only X-linked urea cycle disorder; accumulated carbamoyl phosphate enters cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis, elevating urinary orotic acid.

open.q: Name the deficient enzyme and inheritance pattern of the urea cycle disorder characterized by hyperammonemia with elevated urinary orotic acid.

questions.sub: Organic Acidemias and Urea Cycle Defects
questions.q: How can carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency be biochemically differentiated from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency in a neonate with hyperammonemia?
options: Glutamine is normal in CPS-I deficiency
Orotic acid is low/normal in CPS-I deficiency but raised in OTC deficiency
Hyperammonaemia occurs only after age five
Arginine is markedly raised in CPS-I deficiency
questions.explain: In CPS-I deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate is not synthesized, so none spills over into pyrimidine synthesis and urinary orotic acid remains normal or low.

open.q: How do urinary orotic acid levels differ between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency?
accept: Urinary orotic acid is low or normal in CPS-I deficiency and elevated in OTC deficiency
Elevated in OTC deficiency, normal or low in CPS-I deficiency

questions.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes classic galactosemia?
questions.explain: Galactose 1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) deficiency leads to toxic accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate in liver, kidney, and brain, causing jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis.

open.q: Name the enzyme deficient in classic galactosemia.

questions.q: Why do patients with galactokinase deficiency develop bilateral cataracts in infancy without hepatomegaly or intellectual disability?
options: Excess galactose directly denatures lens crystallins
Galactose 1-phosphate accumulates exclusively in the lens
Deficiency of UDP-galactose impairs corneal collagen
Excess galactose is reduced by lens aldose reductase to osmotically active galactitol
questions.explain: Without galactokinase, galactose is not phosphorylated to toxic galactose 1-phosphate, sparing the liver and brain, but lens aldose reductase converts excess galactose into galactitol, drawing water into lens fibers.

open.q: Name the sugar alcohol responsible for cataract formation in galactokinase deficiency and classic galactosemia.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant develops severe hypoglycemia, vomiting, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly upon weaning onto fruit purees and table sugar. Reducing substances are positive in urine, while glucose oxidase strip is negative. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency, trapping fructose 1-phosphate in hepatocytes and depleting inorganic phosphate needed for ATP regeneration, glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes hereditary fructose intolerance?

questions.q: A 4-month-old infant presents with severe fasting hypoglycemia, doll-like facies, massive hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. Which glycogen storage disease does this represent?
questions.explain: Von Gierke disease (GSD type I) is caused by glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency, impairing both hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

open.q: Name the glycogen storage disease caused by glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency.

questions.q: How does Cori disease (GSD type III, debranching enzyme deficiency) differ clinically and biochemically from Von Gierke disease (GSD type I)?
options: Cori disease causes severe lactic acidosis
Cori disease has milder hypoglycaemia, normal lactate and intact gluconeogenesis
Cori disease affects only skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Because glucose 6-phosphatase and gluconeogenesis remain intact in Cori disease (amylo-1,6-glucosidase deficiency), fasting hypoglycemia is milder and lactate does not accumulate.

open.q: Which enzyme is deficient in Cori disease (glycogen storage disease type III)?

questions.q: Which glycogen storage disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency, leading to massive cardiomegaly and hypotonia in infancy?
questions.explain: Pompe disease (GSD type II) results from lysosomal acid maltase (acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase) deficiency; glycogen accumulates within membrane-bound lysosomes rather than free in the cytoplasm.

open.q: Name the glycogen storage disease caused by lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man experiences painful muscle cramps and dark red-brown urine after sprinting, with no rise in venous lactate during an ischemic forearm exercise test. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: McArdle disease (GSD type V) is caused by skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase) deficiency, blocking muscle glycogen breakdown during intense exercise and causing rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes McArdle disease?

questions.q: Why does glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency predispose erythrocytes to oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies?
options: Low NADPH impairs regeneration of reduced glutathione
questions.explain: Mature red blood cells depend exclusively on G6PD and the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH; without NADPH, glutathione reductase cannot regenerate reduced GSH to detoxify hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing hemoglobin into Heinz bodies.

open.q: Which reducing cofactor becomes depleted in G6PD-deficient erythrocytes, preventing glutathione reduction?

questions.q: An 8-month-old infant presents with progressive loss of motor milestones, exaggerated startle response to noise, and a cherry-red spot on the macula without hepatosplenomegaly. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive deficiency of hexosaminidase A causing GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons, neurodegeneration, and a cherry-red macula without organomegaly.

open.q: Deficiency of which lysosomal enzyme causes Tay-Sachs disease?

questions.q: Which clinical feature reliably distinguishes Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase deficiency) from Tay-Sachs disease in an infant with neurodegeneration and a cherry-red macula?
questions.explain: Both Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease type A present with neurodegeneration and a macular cherry-red spot, but Niemann-Pick disease also exhibits prominent hepatosplenomegaly due to sphingomyelin accumulation in macrophages.

open.q: Name the enzyme deficient in Niemann-Pick disease types A and B.

questions.q: A 12-year-old child presents with hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and aseptic necrosis of the femur. Bone marrow aspirate reveals lipid-laden macrophages resembling 'crinkled tissue paper'. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Gaucher disease is caused by beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency, resulting in glucocerebroside accumulation within macrophages (Gaucher cells) in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes Gaucher disease?

questions.q: Fabry disease is the only X-linked sphingolipidosis and presents with neuropathic limb pain, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, and progressive renal failure due to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, characterized by endothelial accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (ceramide trihexoside).

open.q: Name the X-linked lysosomal enzyme deficient in Fabry disease.

questions.q: Hurler syndrome (MPS I) and Hunter syndrome (MPS II) both involve accumulation of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, but how do they differ clinically and genetically?
options: Hunter syndrome causes more severe corneal clouding
Hunter syndrome is X-linked recessive and lacks corneal clouding
questions.explain: Hurler syndrome (alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency) is autosomal recessive with severe corneal clouding, whereas Hunter syndrome (iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency) is X-linked recessive and typically lacks corneal clouding.

open.q: Name the two glycosaminoglycans that accumulate in both Hurler and Hunter syndromes.

questions.q: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is caused by a defect in Golgi N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, failing to add which targeting marker onto lysosomal acid hydrolases?
questions.explain: Without the mannose 6-phosphate tag, newly synthesized lysosomal enzymes are secreted extracellularly into plasma instead of being trafficked to lysosomes, leaving inclusion bodies inside cells.

open.q: Name the carbohydrate targeting signal missing on lysosomal enzymes in I-cell disease.

questions.q: Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) is caused by defective peroxisome biogenesis (PEX gene mutations), leading to marked plasma accumulation of which lipid class?
questions.explain: Peroxisomes are required for initial beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs, C22+) and plasmalogen synthesis; peroxisomal biogenesis defects cause elevated VLCFAs, hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism, and early death.

open.q: Which class of fatty acids accumulates in plasma in Zellweger syndrome and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with severe hypoketotic hypoglycemia, lethargy, and vomiting triggered by a 16-hour fast during gastroenteritis. Urine shows C6-C10 dicarboxylic aciduria. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: MCAD deficiency impairs mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids, preventing ketogenesis and depriving gluconeogenesis of acetyl-CoA and ATP during fasting.

open.q: Deficiency of which mitochondrial beta-oxidation enzyme causes fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia with C6-C10 dicarboxylic aciduria?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with spasticity, developmental delay, gouty arthritis, and compulsive self-mutilating biting of his lips and fingers. Deficiency of which enzyme causes this X-linked disorder?
questions.explain: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is caused by HGPRT deficiency, impairing purine salvage, elevating PRPP and de novo purine synthesis, and causing severe hyperuricemia and neurobehavioral symptoms.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: An infant with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) has profound T- and B-cell lymphopenia due to toxic dATP accumulation inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase. Which purine catabolic enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency leads to buildup of deoxyadenosine and dATP in lymphocytes, inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase and halting DNA replication.

open.q: Deficiency of which purine degradation enzyme causes autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I presents with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus in the first days of life due to complete absence of which hepatic enzyme?
questions.explain: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is caused by complete absence of bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), preventing bilirubin conjugation and causing fatal kernicterus unless treated with phototherapy and liver transplantation.

open.q: Complete absence of which conjugating enzyme causes Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: A 24-year-old woman develops acute severe abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and hallucinations after starting an oral contraceptive and sulfonamide antibiotic. Her urine turns port-wine red on standing, and she has no skin blisters. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase), causing episodic neurovisceral crises triggered by CYP450 inducers without cutaneous photosensitivity.

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes acute intermittent porphyria?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: A child with fat malabsorption, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, and acanthocytes (spur cells) on peripheral blood smear has undetectable serum ApoB-48 and ApoB-100. Which protein is defective in abetalipoproteinemia?
questions.explain: Abetalipoproteinemia is caused by mutations in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), preventing lipid loading onto ApoB-48 and ApoB-100 to form chylomicrons and VLDL.

open.q: Mutation in which lipid transfer protein causes autosomal recessive abetalipoproteinemia?

questions.q: An infant has seizures, hypotonia, developmental regression, and progressive visual impairment. Testing shows markedly reduced arylsulfatase A activity with sulfatide accumulation in nervous tissue. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explain: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is usually due to autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency, causing sulfatide accumulation and progressive demyelination in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

open.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy?

questions.q: A child develops photophobia, renal Fanconi syndrome, growth failure, and crystals within corneal and conjunctival cells. Which defect causes the underlying disorder?
options: Defective cystine transport out of lysosomes
Failure to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes
questions.explain: Nephropathic cystinosis results from CTNS-related cystinosin dysfunction, impairing cystine export from lysosomes. Cystine accumulates as crystals, causing proximal tubular dysfunction and progressive renal disease; corneal crystals cause photophobia.

open.q: What transport defect causes nephropathic cystinosis?

questions.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
questions.q: A young adult has tendon xanthomas and premature coronary artery disease. His untreated LDL cholesterol is markedly elevated, while triglycerides are near normal. Which inherited defect most commonly causes classic familial hypercholesterolaemia?
options: Reduced function of the LDL receptor
questions.explain: Classic familial hypercholesterolaemia is most often caused by pathogenic variants in LDLR, reducing hepatic clearance of LDL particles. Tendon xanthomas and premature atherosclerotic disease are characteristic; APOB and PCSK9 variants are other causes.

open.q: Which receptor defect most commonly causes classic familial hypercholesterolaemia?

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with tremor, personality change, jaundice, and Kayser-Fleischer rings. Which molecular defect is responsible for the underlying copper accumulation?
options: ATP7B dysfunction impairing biliary copper excretion
ATP7A dysfunction impairing intestinal copper absorption
questions.explain: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive ATP7B disorder. Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary copper excretion cause copper accumulation, especially in liver, brain and cornea.

open.q: Which gene is defective in Wilson disease?

questions.q: A neonate develops metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, ketosis, and an elevated plasma methylmalonic acid concentration. Which enzyme deficiency is a classic cause of isolated methylmalonic acidaemia?
questions.explain: Isolated methylmalonic acidaemia commonly results from deficiency of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or defects in its adenosylcobalamin cofactor pathway. Methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be converted efficiently to succinyl-CoA, leading to methylmalonate accumulation and metabolic decompensation.

open.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes isolated methylmalonic acidaemia?
